extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP litigators, law students, and judges considering design patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether an accused design infringes a design patent under Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent, with emphasis on the appropriate legal test and how to account for prior art and points of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary Observer Test (Gorham)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in the eye of the ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same, if the resemblance is such as to deceive such an observer, inducing him to purchase one supposing it to be the other, the first one patented is infringed by the other. (Gorham Co. v. White, 81 U.S. 511, 528 (1871)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The en banc Federal Circuit in Egyptian Goddess held that the ordinary observer test is the exclusive test for design patent infringement. Apply this test by asking whether an ordinary purchaser, paying the usual amount of attention, would perceive the accused design as the same as the patented design so as to be deceived or induced to purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of Novelty Test (Litton) — previously applied
rubrics_metrics.description: For a design patent to be infringed ... the accused device must appropriate the novelty in the patented device which distinguishes it from the prior art. Even though the court compares two items through the eyes of the ordinary observer, it must nevertheless, to find infringement, attribute their similarity to the novelty which distinguishes the patented device from the prior art. (Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp., 728 F.2d 1423, 144 (Fed. Cir. 1984)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test required identifying the novel features that distinguish the patented design from the prior art and showing the accused product appropriated those novel points. The en banc Egyptian Goddess court rejected this as inconsistent with precedent and unnecessary; therefore, do not treat point-of-novelty as a separate, compulsory test going forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Prior Art as Context for the Ordinary Observer Comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to emphasize the similarities and differences between two designs is to view the designs in light of the prior art from the perspective of an ordinary observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the ordinary observer test, consider how prior art affects the ordinary observer's perception: features common in the prior art may be seen as less distinctive, and what remains distinctive should be evaluated in the overall ordinary-observer comparison rather than isolated as separate 'points of novelty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Reliance on Single Point-of-Novelty Focus (Anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The point of novelty test presents a problem when a design patent contains several points of novelty, namely that any one point of novelty that a court chooses to focus on may determine the outcome of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not structure infringement analysis around isolating one novel element and deciding the case solely on that element; instead, use the holistic ordinary observer approach that weighs overall visual impression in context of prior art to avoid arbitrary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial Similarity Threshold — Deceptive Resemblance Inducing Purchase
rubrics_metrics.description: Two designs are 'substantially the same' if the resemblance is such as to deceive an ordinary observer, inducing him to purchase one supposing it to be the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the overall resemblance would cause confusion in the marketplace for an ordinary purchaser. The inquiry is practical and fact-specific, centered on deception/inducement to purchase rather than abstract feature-by-feature matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's Burden and Standard of Proof: Preponderance of the Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff in a design patent case must show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that an ordinary observer, taking into account the prior art, would believe the accused design to be the same as the patented design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the ordinary observer test under the civil standard of proof (preponderance). In Egyptian Goddess the court held that no reasonable fact-finder could find infringement under this standard given the evidence, affirming summary judgment of noninfringement.
